exam.title: Linear Algebra I - Beginner Exam
exam.subtitle: Fundamentals of linear algebra
exam.instructions: Complete all tasks. Show all calculations and provide the complete solution approach. Permitted aids: non-programmable calculator. Good luck!

exercises.title: Dot product, angle and cross product
exercises.description:
Let $\vec a = (1,2,2)$ and $\vec b = (2,-1,2)$.
a) Compute $\vec a\cdot\vec b$, $|\vec a|$, $|\vec b|$ and the angle between the vectors.
b) Compute $\vec a\times\vec b$ and verify orthogonality to $\vec a$ and $\vec b$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Dot product and lengths
$\vec a\cdot\vec b = 2 - 2 + 4 = 4$. $|\vec a| = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3$, $|\vec b| = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3$.

Step 2: Part a): Angle
$\cos\varphi = \frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec a||\vec b|} = \frac49$, so $\varphi = \arccos\frac49 \approx 63.6^\circ$.

Step 3: Part b): Cross product
$\vec a\times\vec b = (2\cdot2 - 2\cdot(-1),\ 2\cdot2 - 1\cdot2,\ 1\cdot(-1) - 2\cdot2) = (6, 2, -5)$.

Step 4: Part b): Orthogonality check
$(6,2,-5)\cdot\vec a = 6 + 4 - 10 = 0$ ✓ and $(6,2,-5)\cdot\vec b = 12 - 2 - 10 = 0$ ✓. Extra check: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2 = 36 + 4 + 25 = 65 = |\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2\sin^2\varphi = 81\left(1 - \frac{16}{81}\right) = 65$ ✓.

exercises.title: Gaussian elimination
exercises.description:
Solve with Gaussian elimination:
$x + y + z = 6,\quad 2x - y + z = 3,\quad x + 2y - z = 2.$
State the solution set and check it.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Augmented matrix
$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & | & 6 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 & | & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 & | & 2 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 2: Eliminate the first column
$R_2 \to R_2 - 2R_1$, $R_3 \to R_3 - R_1$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & | & 6 \\ 0 & -3 & -1 & | & -9 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & | & -4 \end{pmatrix}$.

Step 3: Eliminate the second column
$R_3 \to R_3 + \frac13R_2$: $(0,\ 0,\ -2 - \tfrac13 \mid -4 - 3) = (0,0,-\tfrac73 \mid -7)$. So $-\frac73z = -7 \Rightarrow z = 3$.

Step 4: Back substitution
Row 2: $-3y - 3 = -9 \Rightarrow y = 2$. Row 1: $x + 2 + 3 = 6 \Rightarrow x = 1$. Solution set: $L = \{(1,2,3)\}$.

Step 5: Check
$1 + 2 + 3 = 6$ ✓; $2 - 2 + 3 = 3$ ✓; $1 + 4 - 3 = 2$ ✓. Three pivots for three unknowns: uniquely solvable.

exercises.title: Matrix operations
exercises.description:
Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$.
a) Compute $AB$, $BA$ and $A^T$.
b) Verify $(AB)^T = B^TA^T$.
c) Describe what multiplication with $B$ from the right resp. left does.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Products and transpose
$AB = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$, $BA = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, $A^T = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$.

Step 2: Part b): Transpose rule
$(AB)^T = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$. $B^TA^T = BA^T = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ ✓. Note the reversed order.

Step 3: Part c): Interpretation
$AB$ arises from $A$ by a **column swap**, $BA$ by a **row swap**. That $AB \neq BA$ shows: matrix multiplication is not commutative.

Step 4: Extra check
$B^2 = I$ (swapping twice gives the identity), i.e. $B$ is its own inverse. $\det B = -1$.

exercises.title: Dependence, basis and dimension
exercises.description:
Let $\vec v_1 = (1,2,1)$, $\vec v_2 = (2,1,0)$, $\vec v_3 = (1,-1,-1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
a) Are the vectors linearly independent? If not, give a dependence.
b) Determine the dimension of $\operatorname{span}\{\vec v_1,\vec v_2,\vec v_3\}$ and a basis.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Set-up
We solve $c_1\vec v_1 + c_2\vec v_2 + c_3\vec v_3 = \vec0$: $c_1 + 2c_2 + c_3 = 0$, $2c_1 + c_2 - c_3 = 0$, $c_1 - c_3 = 0$.

Step 2: Part a): Solve
From the third equation $c_3 = c_1$. First: $2c_1 + 2c_2 = 0 \Rightarrow c_2 = -c_1$. Second: $2c_1 - c_1 - c_1 = 0$ ✓ (automatically satisfied). So there are non-trivial solutions: $(c_1,c_2,c_3) = (1,-1,1)$.

Step 3: Part a): Check
$\vec v_1 - \vec v_2 + \vec v_3 = (1 - 2 + 1,\ 2 - 1 - 1,\ 1 - 0 - 1) = (0,0,0)$ ✓. The vectors are **linearly dependent**: $\vec v_3 = \vec v_2 - \vec v_1$.

Step 4: Part b): Basis and dimension
$\vec v_3$ is redundant. $\vec v_1,\vec v_2$ are not proportional, hence linearly independent. Basis $\{\vec v_1,\vec v_2\}$, $\dim\operatorname{span} = 2$ (a plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$). Check: $\det(\vec v_1,\vec v_2,\vec v_3) = 0$.

exercises.title: Inverse of a 3×3 matrix
exercises.description: Determine the inverse of $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ with Gauss-Jordan elimination and verify the result.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Determinant as a pre-test
Expansion along the first row: $\det A = 1(1\cdot1 - 1\cdot0) - 2(0\cdot1 - 1\cdot1) = 1 + 2 = 3 \neq 0$. The inverse exists.

Step 2: Start (A mid I) and forward elimination
$R_3 \to R_3 - R_1$: $(0,-2,1 \mid -1,0,1)$. Then $R_3 \to R_3 + 2R_2$: $(0,0,3 \mid -1,2,1)$.

Step 3: Normalise and eliminate upwards
$R_3 \to \frac13R_3$: $(0,0,1 \mid -\tfrac13,\tfrac23,\tfrac13)$. $R_2 \to R_2 - R_3$: $(0,1,0 \mid \tfrac13,\tfrac13,-\tfrac13)$. $R_1 \to R_1 - 2R_2$: $(1,0,0 \mid \tfrac13,-\tfrac23,\tfrac23)$.

Step 4: Result
$A^{-1} = \frac13\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

Step 5: Check
First row of $A$ times columns of $3A^{-1}$: $(1,2,0)\cdot(1,1,-1) = 3$ ✓, $(1,2,0)\cdot(-2,1,2) = 0$ ✓, $(1,2,0)\cdot(2,-1,1) = 0$ ✓. So $AA^{-1} = I$ in the first row.

exercises.title: Determinants and Cramer's rule
exercises.description:
a) Compute $\det\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&3&2\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}$ with the rule of Sarrus.
b) Solve $3x + 2y = 7$, $x - y = 1$ with Cramer's rule.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Sarrus
Descending diagonals: $2\cdot3\cdot1 + 1\cdot2\cdot0 + 0\cdot1\cdot1 = 6$. Ascending: $0\cdot3\cdot0 + 2\cdot2\cdot1 + 1\cdot1\cdot1 = 5$. $\det = 6 - 5 = 1$.

Step 2: Part a): Check
Expansion along the first row: $2(3 - 2) - 1(1 - 0) + 0 = 2 - 1 = 1$ ✓. Since $\det \neq 0$ the matrix is invertible.

Step 3: Part b): Cramer's rule
$\det A = \begin{vmatrix}3&2\\1&-1\end{vmatrix} = -3 - 2 = -5 \neq 0$. $x = \frac{\begin{vmatrix}7&2\\1&-1\end{vmatrix}}{-5} = \frac{-7 - 2}{-5} = \frac95$, $y = \frac{\begin{vmatrix}3&7\\1&1\end{vmatrix}}{-5} = \frac{3 - 7}{-5} = \frac45$.

Step 4: Part b): Check
$3\cdot\frac95 + 2\cdot\frac45 = \frac{27 + 8}{5} = 7$ ✓ and $\frac95 - \frac45 = 1$ ✓.
